anxiety-disorders.name: Anxiety and generalised anxiety disorder
anxiety-disorders.definition: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is a long-term condition in which a person feels worried or anxious about many different things, much of the time.
anxiety-disorders.overview: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is a long-term condition in which a person worries about many situations rather than one specific event. The NHS describes persistent stress or worry that is hard to control and disrupts daily life, often alongside physical symptoms such as trouble sleeping, tiredness, dizziness or palpitations. The NHS says it affects more women than men. A GP can assess the symptoms, and NICE describes a stepped approach to treatment.
causes: The exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, and a combination of several factors is likely to be involved.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists says there is no single cause, and that genes, social environment and life experiences all play a role and interact with each other.
A history of stressful or traumatic experiences is described as a possible contributor.
riskFactors: Having close relatives with anxiety, depression or other mental health conditions.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists says a close family member with GAD makes an anxiety disorder several times more likely, although no single gene is responsible.
A history of stressful or traumatic experiences.
GAD affects more women than men.
signs: Feeling restless or worried.
Difficulty concentrating.
Feeling tense.
complications: Persistent worry that disrupts daily life and is hard to control.
Trouble sleeping and getting tired easily.
anxiety-disorders.diagnosis: The NHS says a GP will ask about a person's worries, emotions and symptoms. A person is most likely to be diagnosed with GAD if symptoms have lasted six months or more. The GP may carry out a physical examination or blood tests to rule out other conditions that could cause the symptoms, such as an overactive thyroid gland. The NHS notes that it can be difficult to tell GAD apart from other mental health conditions, such as depression.
anxiety-disorders.treatment: NICE describes a stepped approach that offers the least intrusive, most effective intervention first. It starts with education and active monitoring in primary care. The next step covers low-intensity options such as self-help and psychoeducational groups. Higher steps include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) or applied relaxation. NICE says benzodiazepines should not be offered except as a short-term measure in a crisis, and that antipsychotics should not be offered in primary care. The Royal College of Psychiatrists describes SSRI antidepressants as a medicine option, with an SNRI that may be offered if SSRIs do not work.
anxiety-disorders.prevention: The sources checked do not describe a sure way to prevent GAD, and the NHS says its exact cause is not fully understood.
anxiety-disorders.seekCare: A GP appointment is the usual route when anxiety is ongoing or affects daily life. If someone is in crisis but not in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) is available 24 hours a day. If there is immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E. Samaritans on 116 123 is free and open 24 hours every day.

sections.heading: What is generalised anxiety disorder?
sections.body:
Generalised anxiety disorder, often shortened to GAD, is a long-term condition. The NHS and NHS inform describe it as worry about many situations rather than about one specific event. The central feature is persistent stress or worry that is hard to control and that disrupts daily life.

The NHS says that more women than men are affected, and that the condition is most common between the ages of 35 and 55. Those descriptions come from NHS pages written about adults.

GAD can be hard to separate from other mental health conditions. The NHS notes that it can be difficult to tell GAD apart from conditions such as depression. For this reason a GP looks at a person's worries, emotions and symptoms together, rather than at a single feature. The sections below set out what the sources say about the symptoms, causes, diagnosis and treatment of GAD, and when to seek help.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of GAD?
sections.body:
The main feature of GAD is persistent stress or worry that is hard to control and that disrupts daily life. The NHS describes symptoms that affect both thoughts and the body.

Symptoms can include feeling restless or worried, having trouble concentrating, and having trouble sleeping. Physical symptoms described in NHS material include getting tired easily, feeling tense, stomach problems, feeling lightheaded or dizzy, and heart palpitations.

The NHS has a separate page on the signs of an anxiety disorder for readers who want a fuller list. The symptoms above are described as part of GAD when the worry is persistent, hard to control and disruptive to daily life. A person who recognises these symptoms in themselves or in someone close to them can talk to a GP about them.

sections.heading: What causes generalised anxiety disorder?
sections.body:
The NHS says the exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, and that a combination of several factors is likely to be involved. A history of stressful or traumatic experiences is described as one possible contributor.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists says GAD does not have a single cause. It describes genes, social environment and life experiences as all playing a role, and as interacting with each other.

Family history is mentioned by both organisations. The NHS says that close relatives with anxiety, depression or other mental health conditions raise the risk. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says that having a close family member with GAD makes an anxiety disorder several times more likely. It adds that no single gene is responsible. Instead, several genes that each have a small effect combine to raise the risk. None of this means that a person is to blame for feeling anxious.

sections.heading: How is GAD diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says that a GP will ask about a person's worries, emotions and symptoms. A person is most likely to be diagnosed with GAD if the symptoms have lasted six months or more.

To help with the diagnosis, the GP may carry out a physical examination or blood tests. These are used to rule out other conditions that could be causing the symptoms, such as an overactive thyroid gland. The NHS also notes that it can be difficult to tell GAD apart from other mental health conditions, such as depression, which is one reason the GP asks about the full picture.

NICE describes a stepped approach to care. It starts with education about GAD and active monitoring in primary care. Further steps are offered for GAD that has not improved after that first stage, as the next section explains.

sections.heading: How is GAD treated?
sections.body:
NICE describes a stepped approach that offers the least intrusive, most effective intervention first. The first stage in primary care is education and active monitoring. For GAD that has not improved after that, the next step covers low-intensity options such as self-help and psychoeducational groups.

Higher steps include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) or applied relaxation, which are psychological treatments. NICE says the guideline does not recommend one particular method of CBT over another. For complex GAD that has not responded to treatment and that causes very marked difficulty in daily life, NICE describes highly specialist treatment.

On medicines, NICE says benzodiazepines should not be offered for GAD except as a short-term measure in a crisis, and antipsychotics should not be offered in primary care. The Royal College of Psychiatrists describes SSRI antidepressants as a medicine option, with an SNRI that may be offered if SSRIs do not work. The clinician decides with the person which options suit them.

sections.heading: When should someone get help?
sections.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route when anxiety is ongoing or affects daily life. The GP can ask about the symptoms and discuss the options described above.

If someone is in crisis but not in immediate danger, NHS 111 is available 24 hours a day and offers a mental health option for urgent mental health help. The number for that option varies by area, so it is chosen from the options on the call.

If there is immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E. Samaritans can be reached free on 116 123, and the line is open 24 hours every day, for anyone who needs someone to talk to. These routes are for moments of crisis, while the GP is the route for ongoing anxiety.

faqs.q: Can GAD be treated?
faqs.a: Yes, NICE describes a stepped approach to treating GAD. It starts with education and active monitoring, then low-intensity options such as self-help and psychoeducational groups, then CBT or applied relaxation. Medicines are also described in the guidance, including SSRI antidepressants. The clinician decides with the person which options suit them.

faqs.q: Does a family history of anxiety mean someone will develop GAD?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says a close family member with GAD makes an anxiety disorder several times more likely, but that no single gene is responsible. Genes, social environment and life experiences all play a role and interact. The NHS says the exact cause of GAD is not fully understood.

faqs.q: How long do symptoms last before GAD is diagnosed?
faqs.a: The NHS says a person is most likely to be diagnosed with GAD if they have had symptoms for six months or more. A GP asks about worries, emotions and symptoms, and may arrange a physical examination or blood tests to rule out other conditions, such as an overactive thyroid gland.

faqs.q: Does GAD affect men and women equally?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says GAD affects more women than men, and that it is most common between the ages of 35 and 55. The NHS notes that GAD can be difficult to tell apart from other mental health conditions such as depression, so a GP looks at the whole picture.

faqs.q: Who can someone talk to in a crisis?
faqs.a: Anyone in immediate danger should call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 offers a mental health option and is available 24 hours a day. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123, open 24 hours every day. A GP appointment is the usual route for ongoing anxiety.

depression.name: Depression
depression.definition: Depression is a low mood that lasts for weeks or months and affects daily life.
depression.overview: Depression is a low mood that lasts for weeks or months and affects daily life. Symptoms vary a lot between people and range from mild to severe. They can be psychological, such as continuous low mood and hopelessness, or physical, such as feeling constantly tired and sleeping badly. Self-help, talking therapies and antidepressant medicines are among the treatments the NHS describes, and the choice depends on how severe the depression is.
causes: The NHS says there is often a trigger for depression.
The NHS lists stressful events, personality and giving birth among the factors, and says grief after bereavement can bring on symptoms of depression.
MedlinePlus lists genetic, biological, environmental and psychological factors as possible causes.
Certain medicines and medical conditions, such as viruses or thyroid disorders, can cause symptoms like those of depression, according to NIMH and MedlinePlus.
riskFactors: A family history of depression raises the likelihood of experiencing it, according to the NHS.
Stressful events and giving birth are listed by the NHS among the factors linked to depression.
signs: Continuous low mood, hopelessness and low self-esteem.
Avoiding contact with friends and taking part in fewer social activities.
Poor sleep, changes in appetite and constant tiredness.
complications: Severe depression can make a person feel suicidal or feel that life is no longer worth living.
Some people have psychotic depression, and NHS inform says they might be at higher risk of thinking about suicide.
depression.diagnosis: There is no physical test that diagnoses depression. The NHS says a GP may examine the person and arrange some urine or blood tests to rule out other conditions with similar symptoms, such as an underactive thyroid. The GP also asks about medical history, previous mental health problems, home environment and lifestyle, recent triggers such as stressful events, and any thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
depression.treatment: Treatment is based on how severe the depression is. For mild depression, a GP may suggest watchful waiting, in which progress is monitored, along with exercise or guided self-help. Talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) can also be used. For moderate to severe depression, a combination of talking therapy and antidepressants is often recommended. NICE advises against routinely offering antidepressants first for less severe depression unless the person prefers them. A GP will usually prescribe a type of antidepressant called a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) if one is thought likely to help, and the NHS names sertraline and citalopram among them. The NHS says people can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service without a GP referral.
depression.prevention: The NHS and Mind describe regular exercise, not drinking too much alcohol, eating and drinking regularly and sharing experiences with other people as ways of looking after mood.
depression.seekCare: If someone is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help with thoughts of suicide, NHS 111 is available 24 hours a day (use the mental health option), and Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time. A GP appointment is the routine route when symptoms of depression last most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks.

sections.heading: What is depression, and how is it different from low mood?
sections.body:
Depression is a low mood that lasts for weeks or months and affects daily life. The NHS says a low mood may improve after a short period of time, and that this is not necessarily a sign of depression. It advises seeing a GP when symptoms of depression last for most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks. Symptoms vary a lot between people and range from mild to severe. The NHS notes that severe depression can make a person feel suicidal, or feel that life is no longer worth living.

Mind describes several forms of depression. Persistent depressive disorder is continuous depression that lasts for two years or more. Seasonal affective disorder is depression that occurs at a particular time of year or during a particular season. Antenatal depression occurs during pregnancy, and postnatal depression occurs in the first year after having a baby.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of depression?
sections.body:
Symptoms vary a lot from person to person, and the NHS groups them as psychological, physical and social. Psychological symptoms include continuous low mood, hopelessness, low self-esteem and feeling tearful. Suicidal thoughts are also listed among the psychological symptoms.

Physical symptoms include feeling constantly tired, sleeping badly, changes in appetite or weight, usually a decrease, and unexplained aches and pains. Social effects include avoiding contact with friends and taking part in fewer social activities.

Some people have psychotic depression. NHS inform says that a person with psychotic depression might be at higher risk of thinking about suicide. Anyone who has these thoughts, or who is worried about someone else, can use the crisis routes described at the end of this article.

sections.heading: What causes depression, and how is it diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is often a trigger for depression, and that a family history raises the likelihood of experiencing it. Other factors it lists include stressful events, personality and giving birth. It notes that grief after bereavement can bring on symptoms of depression, although these usually ease over time. MedlinePlus lists genetic, biological, environmental and psychological factors as possible causes. NIMH and MedlinePlus add that certain medicines and medical conditions, such as viruses or thyroid disorders, can cause symptoms like those of depression. The NHS lists low mood as a common symptom of an underactive thyroid.

There is no physical test that diagnoses depression. The GP asks about medical history, previous mental health problems, home environment and lifestyle, recent triggers such as stressful events, and any thoughts of suicide or self-harm. The NHS says a GP may examine the person and arrange some urine or blood tests to rule out other conditions with similar symptoms, such as an underactive thyroid. MedlinePlus says blood tests may look for conditions such as anaemia or thyroid disease.

sections.heading: How is depression treated?
sections.body:
Treatment is based on how severe the depression is. For mild depression, the NHS says a GP may suggest watchful waiting, which means monitoring progress to see whether it improves on its own. Exercise and guided self-help may also be suggested. The NHS says guided self-help usually involves six to eight sessions of working through a workbook or online course with support from a therapist. Talking therapies such as CBT can also be used for mild depression, particularly if it is not improving.

For moderate to severe depression, a combination of talking therapy and antidepressants is often recommended. Severe cases may go to a specialist team that provides intensive talking treatments as well as prescribed medicine.

NICE says guided self-help is the suggested first step for most people with less severe depression, and that the evidence for group CBT and group behavioural activation was good. NICE advises against routinely offering antidepressants first for less severe depression unless that is the person's preference. The NHS also describes interpersonal therapy, counselling and behavioural couples therapy. The NHS says people can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service without a GP referral, although services vary by area and cannot provide urgent mental health help.

sections.heading: What do antidepressants involve?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP will usually prescribe a type of antidepressant called a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) if one is thought likely to help. It names sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine and citalopram as commonly used examples. NICE considers SSRIs the preferred antidepressant if one is chosen, because of their safety and tolerability.

The NHS says SSRIs work about as well as older antidepressants with fewer side effects, although they can still cause nausea, headaches, a dry mouth, tiredness, sleeping problems and problems with sex. Tricyclic antidepressants are older options used for moderate to severe depression. The NHS says symptoms start to improve within four weeks of starting an antidepressant, and that if it is working, it is continued for at least four to six months after symptoms have eased.

The NHS pages for sertraline and citalopram advise against stopping suddenly, because withdrawal symptoms can occur. They also say these medicines are not addictive in the way that illegal drugs and cigarettes are.

sections.heading: Living with depression and self-help
sections.body:
The NHS lists exercise as one of the main treatments for mild depression, and includes not drinking too much alcohol among its tips for coping with depression. Self-help is described as one part of care, alongside talking therapies and medicines where these are needed.

Mind suggests aiming to wake up and go to bed at the same time each day, and eating and drinking regularly. Mind also notes that sharing experiences with other people can help someone feel better, and that having someone listen and show they care can help in itself.

The NHS says people can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service for CBT or counselling, and that after contact someone from the service usually gets in touch within a few weeks. Waiting times for talking therapies can be several weeks or months, so a GP can discuss other options in the meantime.

sections.heading: Thoughts of suicide and where to get help
sections.body:
Severe depression can make a person feel suicidal, and the NHS says help is available. If someone is in immediate danger, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

Samaritans can be called free on 116 123, and the line is open 24 hours a day, every day. NHS 111 is also available 24 hours a day, and the NHS lists it for urgent mental health help. The number to press for the mental health option varies by area, so the option is described here by name rather than number.

A GP appointment is the routine route when symptoms of depression last for most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks. A GP can discuss treatment options, including talking therapies and antidepressants, and can refer a person to talking therapies, although people can also refer themselves. Talking therapy services are not able to provide urgent help, so anyone in a crisis is directed to the routes above.

faqs.q: Is depression the same as feeling sad?
faqs.a: The NHS describes depression as a low mood that lasts for weeks or months and affects daily life. It says a low mood may improve after a short period of time, which is not necessarily a sign of depression. Symptoms can also be physical, such as constant tiredness and poor sleep, and the NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms last most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks.

faqs.q: Can depression be treated?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS describes treatment that depends on severity. Mild depression may be managed with watchful waiting, exercise, guided self-help or talking therapies such as CBT. Moderate to severe depression is often treated with a combination of talking therapy and antidepressants. A GP can discuss which options may suit the person.

faqs.q: Is a GP referral needed for talking therapy?
faqs.a: The NHS says people can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service without a referral from a GP, and a GP can also refer them. Services vary by area, and the NHS says talking therapies cannot provide urgent mental health help, so people with more severe difficulties are directed to a GP.

faqs.q: How long do antidepressants take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says symptoms start to improve within four weeks of starting an antidepressant. If it is working, treatment is continued for at least four to six months after symptoms have eased. SSRIs can cause side effects such as nausea, headaches, a dry mouth, tiredness and sleeping problems. The NHS advises against stopping sertraline or citalopram suddenly, because withdrawal symptoms can occur.

faqs.q: Where can someone get help with thoughts of suicide?
faqs.a: If someone is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123, 24 hours a day, every day. NHS 111 is also available 24 hours a day, and the NHS lists it for urgent mental health help; the mental health option is chosen from the menu. A GP appointment is the routine route for ongoing symptoms.

adhd.definition: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, activity levels and impulse control.

The NHS says its symptoms usually start before the age of 12, and most people with ADHD have symptoms of both the inattentive type and the hyperactive-impulsive type. sections.heading: What is ADHD and what causes it?
sections.body:
ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, activity levels and impulse control. The NHS says its symptoms usually start before the age of 12, and most people with ADHD have symptoms of both the inattentive type and the hyperactive-impulsive type. A review in the medical literature attributes ADHD to differences in brain structure and function as well as genetic factors.

The NHS says ADHD often runs in families, and that genetic differences may be behind it. The NHS also lists being born prematurely, low birth weight and epilepsy as other possible links. The exact cause is not known. Earlier theories that diet causes hyperactivity are not supported by recent research, according to the NHS sources reviewed. NICE says ADHD is thought to be under-recognised in girls and women, who are less likely to be referred for assessment and may be more likely to receive a different diagnosis. Girls more often show inattentive symptoms, which can be harder to recognise.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of ADHD?
sections.body:
ADHD symptoms are usually grouped into two kinds: inattentiveness, and hyperactivity and impulsiveness. NHS inform lists practical signs of inattentiveness such as getting easily distracted, losing or misplacing things and starting many tasks without finishing them. The NHS describes adult ADHD as affecting focus, with inattentive, restless and impulsive traits. ADHD affects people in different ways.

If symptoms are affecting studies, work or relationships, the NHS advises making a GP appointment. The Royal College of Psychiatrists describes the diagnostic criteria as symptoms that have been present since childhood, persist, and cause at least moderate impairment across two or more areas of life: home, work, education and relationships. A large proportion of adults with ADHD have another condition too, such as anxiety, depression, autism, a tic condition such as Tourette syndrome, substance use, or physical health problems including chronic pain and fatigue.

sections.heading: How is ADHD assessed and diagnosed?
sections.body:
There is no single test for ADHD. For children, NICE says primary care practitioners should not make the initial diagnosis or start medication. If problems persist with at least moderate impairment, they refer to secondary care, such as a child psychiatrist, a paediatrician or a specialist ADHD child and adolescent mental health service. NICE says the diagnosis must be made by a specialist psychiatrist, paediatrician or other appropriately qualified healthcare professional.

For adults, the GP asks about the symptoms and how they affect life, and may consider other conditions that could be causing them, such as autism, Tourette's syndrome or anxiety. A specialist assessment asks about the history of symptoms, particularly whether they started in childhood and how they affected school. An adult diagnosis cannot be confirmed unless symptoms have been present since childhood. NICE says a diagnosis should not be made solely on the basis of rating scale or observational data, although rating scales are helpful added tools. The Royal College of Psychiatrists likewise says an ADHD diagnosis should never be based solely on questionnaires. NICE also says clinicians should discuss the positive and negative impacts of receiving a diagnosis, such as stigma and labelling.

sections.heading: How is ADHD treated and supported?
sections.body:
The NHS says ADHD in adults is managed through lifestyle changes, workplace adjustments or medicines, and talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) or mindfulness may be recommended. ADHD medicines must be started and monitored by an ADHD specialist. The GP may later take over prescribing under a shared care agreement, although this is the GP's decision and not every practice does it. NICE advises local protocols for shared care with primary care and a written treatment plan shared with the person with ADHD.

NICE notes that for some people symptoms and impairment may be reduced through environmental modifications, such as a modified school curriculum or choice of employment. The guideline asks for modifications to be checked before medication starts. A European consensus statement on adult ADHD advises multimodal treatment made up of psychoeducation, pharmacotherapy, coaching and/or CBT, ideally involving the person's partner, family or close friends. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says early years support and reasonable adjustments at school and work can help reduce the impact that ADHD has on people's lives.

sections.heading: Living with ADHD
sections.body:
ADHD affects people in different ways, and the Royal College of Psychiatrists' information for adults covers both the challenges and the strengths people with ADHD can have. A 2023 thematic analysis of adults' positive experiences found that being creative, having novel ideas, seeing things from a different perspective and being good at finding solutions were commonly described as strengths. A MedlinePlus support guide describes ADHD as a lifelong journey and says understanding and acceptance from others can make a world of difference.

ADHD UK provides information and support for anyone affected by ADHD, including a self-screening tool and support groups. Waiting times for specialist adult ADHD services vary, and in some areas it can take several months or years to be seen. ADHD UK says that if the local wait is long, a GP can refer to another NHS-approved provider under Right to Choose, although some areas limit the scheme and it is worth checking locally.

sections.heading: When should you get help?
sections.body:
If ADHD symptoms are affecting studies, work or relationships, the NHS advises making a GP appointment to find out what support is available. ADHD UK says that if a GP declines a referral, options include asking for a second opinion from a different GP. For a child, NICE says that when problems persist with at least moderate impairment, primary care refers on to a specialist such as a child psychiatrist or paediatrician. Depression and anxiety are among the conditions that can occur alongside ADHD, and people with ADHD often seek treatment for them.

If someone is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help, NHS 111 is available 24 hours, and you can choose the mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123, open 24 hours every day.

faqs.q: Can ADHD be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says ADHD in adults is managed through lifestyle changes, workplace adjustments or medicines. A MedlinePlus support guide describes ADHD as a lifelong journey. Treatment and support therefore aim to help with symptoms and everyday life, and talking therapies such as CBT or mindfulness may also be recommended.

faqs.q: Does ADHD only affect children?
faqs.a: No, the NHS has separate guidance for adults and for children and young people. Symptoms usually start before the age of 12, but an adult can still be assessed. For an adult diagnosis, symptoms must have been present since childhood. Adults with ADHD often have another condition too, such as anxiety or depression.

faqs.q: Can a GP diagnose ADHD?
faqs.a: For children, NICE says primary care practitioners should not make the initial diagnosis or start medication. If problems persist with at least moderate impairment, they refer to secondary care, such as a child psychiatrist or paediatrician. There is no single test, and the NHS says the GP asks about symptoms and how they affect life and may consider other conditions.

faqs.q: Why is ADHD thought to be missed in girls?
faqs.a: NICE says ADHD is thought to be under-recognised in girls and women, who are less likely to be referred for assessment and may be more likely to receive a different diagnosis. Girls more often show inattentive symptoms, which can be harder to recognise. Anyone worried about symptoms that affect studies, work or relationships can start with a GP appointment, as the NHS advises.

autism.name: Autism
autism.definition: A lifelong difference in how a person communicates, behaves and reacts compared with people who are not autistic.
autism.overview: Autism is a lifelong condition that affects how a person communicates, behaves and reacts compared with people who are not autistic. Each autistic person has their own experiences, and signs may be noticed at a very young age or not until later in life. The NHS describes common signs in children and adults, such as differences in communication, repetitive movements, sensory differences and distress at changes in routine. Autism is a difference rather than an illness, and there is no cure. A diagnosis comes from an assessment by a team of health professionals, usually after a referral from a GP.
causes: Genes are thought to play a large part in autism.

A Danish registry study found that valproate, an anti-seizure medicine, taken by mothers during pregnancy was linked to a significantly increased risk of autism, even after allowing for maternal epilepsy.
The National Autistic Society describes valproate exposure in pregnancy as a rare cause now, because prescribing is restricted.
One review found little evidence that environmental factors play a significant role, and noted that most infants exposed before birth to such drugs or chemicals do not develop autism.
riskFactors: Exposure to valproate, an anti-seizure medicine, during pregnancy.
signs: Differences in communication, such as not responding to their name or less eye contact.
Repetitive movements such as hand flapping or rocking.
Being worried or upset by changes in routine or surroundings.
Sensory differences, such as distress at certain sounds or textures.
In adults, getting very anxious about social situations or finding it hard to make friends or preferring to be on their own.
complications: Masking, which means adapting so that signs are not always noticeable, can make everyday activities and social interactions feel exhausting and stressful.
Other conditions such as anxiety, depression, an eating disorder or ADHD can occur alongside autism and can make the signs harder to see.
autism.diagnosis: The NHS says there is no definitive sign or list of signs that can show whether someone is autistic; autism is assessed by clinicians who gather information on multiple signs. For children under 5 a health visitor can be contacted. NICE guidance for under 19s covers recognition, referral and diagnosis from birth up to 19 years.
autism.treatment: The NHS describes support options for the time before and after an assessment. While waiting for an assessment, the NHS suggests speaking to teachers or the SENCO at school, to a manager or HR at work, or asking the local council for a needs assessment. A GP or education professional can say what support is available in the meantime. Telling people close to the person about autism can help them understand how to support them.
autism.prevention: Autism is a lifelong condition. The National Autistic Society says valproate exposure in pregnancy is now a rare cause of autism because prescribing of valproate is restricted.
autism.seekCare: The NHS suggests consulting a GP, or a health professional already seen, for anyone who thinks they or their child may be autistic; the GP can arrange further assessment if needed. A GP appointment is the usual first step, and for a child under 5 a health visitor can also be contacted. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option that connects to a local NHS crisis line, free and open 24 hours a day. If someone is in immediate danger, has seriously harmed themselves or may be about to, call 999 or go to A&E. Samaritans can be called free at any time on 116 123.

sections.heading: What is autism?
sections.body:
Autism is a lifelong condition that affects how a person communicates, behaves and reacts. The NHS describes the main signs as differences in how someone communicates, behaves and reacts compared with people who are not autistic.

The NHS says signs might be noticed at a very young age, or not until later in life.

The NHS also says there is no definitive sign, or list of signs, that can show whether someone is autistic. Instead, autism is assessed by clinicians who gather information on multiple signs. This is why a formal assessment by a team of health professionals matters. The sections below describe the signs the NHS lists for children and for adults, how assessment works, what is known about causes, and where to turn for help, including in a crisis.

sections.heading: What are the signs of autism in children?
sections.body:
The NHS lists signs in how a child communicates, behaves and responds to the world. Examples of communication differences include not responding to their name and using eye contact less often. Another NHS page mentions not smiling or responding to other people's facial expressions, and a preference for playing alone.

Repetitive movements, sometimes called stimming, are also described. They include rocking, spinning, flapping the hands and flicking the fingers. The NHS notes that these movements can also be a way to calm down or to handle excitement.

Autistic children may be worried or upset by changes in routine, by their environment, or by new situations, and some have strong emotional reactions to a change in routine.

Sensory differences are common in the NHS descriptions. A child may react strongly, or not at all, to lights, sounds, smells, tastes or textures, and some children eat only a limited range of foods because of texture or how food is served.

Autism can look different in girls. The NHS says autistic girls may hide some signs by copying how other children behave and play, and may show fewer repetitive behaviours than autistic boys. This can make diagnosis harder, so a girl's needs may be missed.

sections.heading: What are the signs of autism in adults?
sections.body:
The NHS lists signs in adults that include getting very anxious about social situations and finding it hard to make friends or preferring to be on their own. Other NHS pages mention that autistic people may be unsure how much eye contact to use, that making small talk is often hard, and that socialising can leave adults exhausted.

The NHS explains that some people learn to adapt so that signs are not always noticeable. This is called masking, and it can make everyday activities and social interactions feel exhausting and stressful. NHS inform adds that masking is not a conscious choice, and that an autistic person may not be able to start or stop masking at will.

The NHS says women may copy how other people behave, appear to cope well in social situations, be very quiet in difficult situations and hide their feelings, and show fewer repetitive behaviours than autistic men. It may also be harder to see signs of autism if an adult has other conditions such as anxiety, depression, an eating disorder or ADHD.

An NHS trust describes a short questionnaire called the AQ10, which gives only a general indication of whether someone might be autistic.

sections.heading: What causes autism?
sections.body:
The sources used here describe only some of what has been studied about the causes of autism.

Valproate is an anti-seizure medicine. A Danish registry study found that maternal use of valproate during pregnancy was linked to a significantly increased risk of autism spectrum disorders, even after allowing for maternal epilepsy. The National Autistic Society describes valproate exposure in pregnancy as a rare cause now, because prescribing of valproate is restricted.

A review of antenatal factors found little evidence that environmental exposures play a significant role in causing autism. The same review noted that most infants who were exposed before birth to such drugs or chemicals do not develop autism.

Because there is a lot of public discussion about causes, it is worth saying that the sources checked for this page do not describe a single cause that applies to all autistic people.

sections.heading: How is autism assessed and diagnosed?
sections.body:
Autism is usually diagnosed by an assessment from a team of health professionals. Referral usually comes through a GP, or, for children, through a school's special educational needs coordinator (SENCO). NHS inform advises contacting the GP practice if a child might be autistic and a formal assessment is needed, and a health visitor or GP can be contacted for children under 5. The NHS says it is possible to wait a few months for an appointment.

The NHS describes a second opinion as an option if a GP is reluctant to refer. Private assessments are also possible, and a referral from a GP or other NHS professional is not needed to request a private or independent assessment.

NICE guidance for under 19s covers recognition and diagnosis from birth up to 19 years. It asks providers to set up a single point of referral to the autism team. Practitioners are told to consider referral when they have concerns about possible autism based on reported or observed features. NICE says that a positive score on a screening tool may support a decision to refer but can also reflect reasons other than autism, and that a negative score does not rule out autism.

sections.heading: Support while waiting and when to get help
sections.body:
The NHS suggests that while waiting for an assessment, a person can speak to teachers or the SENCO at school, to a manager or human resources at work, and can ask the local council for a needs assessment. A GP or education professional can say what support is available in the meantime. The NHS says telling people close to the person about their or their child's autism can help them understand how to support them.

The NHS advises consulting a GP, or a health professional already seen, if someone thinks they or their child may be autistic. A GP appointment is the usual first step.

For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option that connects to a local NHS crisis line, free and open 24 hours a day. If someone is in immediate danger, has seriously harmed themselves or may be about to, call 999 or go to A&E. Samaritans can be called free at any time on 116 123 by anyone who wants to talk, including people who feel suicidal.

faqs.q: Is autism lifelong?
faqs.a: The NHS describes autism as a lifelong condition. It affects how a person communicates, behaves and reacts compared with people who are not autistic. Signs might be noticed at a very young age, or not until later in life, and an assessment by a team of health professionals is how autism is diagnosed.

faqs.q: How does someone get an autism assessment?
faqs.a: Referral usually comes through a GP, or through a school's special educational needs coordinator for children. A team of health professionals carries out the assessment, because the NHS says no single sign or list of signs shows whether someone is autistic. There can be a wait of a few months, and private assessments are also possible without a GP referral.

faqs.q: Why can autism be missed in girls and women?
faqs.a: The NHS says autistic girls may hide some signs of autism by copying how other children behave and play, and may show fewer repetitive behaviours than autistic boys. Women may copy others, appear to cope well in social situations and hide their feelings. This can make diagnosis harder, so their needs may be missed.

faqs.q: What is masking?
faqs.a: The NHS describes masking as learning to adapt so that signs of autism are not always noticeable. It can make everyday activities and social interactions feel exhausting and stressful. NHS inform adds that masking is not a conscious choice, and that an autistic person may not be able to start or stop masking at will.

faqs.q: What is the AQ10 questionnaire?
faqs.a: An NHS trust page describes the AQ10 as a short questionnaire that can be completed to give a general indication of whether someone might have autism. It is not a diagnosis. The NHS says autism is assessed by clinicians who gather information on multiple signs, and a GP is the usual first step if someone thinks they may be autistic.

ocd.name: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)
ocd.definition: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental health condition in which a person has obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours.
ocd.overview: OCD involves obsessions, which are unwanted and distressing thoughts, images or urges, and compulsions, which are repeated behaviours or mental acts done to ease the anxiety they cause. OCD can affect men, women and children. Symptoms can start from as early as age 6, but they often begin around puberty and early adulthood. The main treatments are talking therapy, usually cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and medicine, usually a type of antidepressant called an SSRI.
causes: MedlinePlus says the cause of OCD is unknown.
Mind says there are different theories about why someone develops OCD, and that no theory can fully explain every person's experience. It points to personal experiences and biological factors.
MedlinePlus says genetics, brain biology and chemistry, and the environment may all play a role.
The NHS says OCD is more likely if a family member has it.
riskFactors: Having a family member with OCD.
Life events such as bullying, abuse, neglect, childbirth or bereavement.
Personality traits such as being meticulous or having a very strong sense of responsibility may be linked to a higher chance of OCD, according to the NHS.
signs: Repeated behaviours such as excessive handwashing, checking or counting, which NHS trust pages list as examples.
Mental compulsions, such as silently repeating a word or phrase, which are not obvious to other people.
Anxiety, disgust or unease linked to unwanted thoughts, images or urges.
Repeatedly asking other people for reassurance, which Mind describes as a very common compulsion.
complications: The NHS says obsessive thoughts and compulsions can affect daily life.
Mind describes relief from a compulsion as short-lived: the thought returns and the cycle repeats.
ocd.diagnosis: The NHS says a person who is affected can see a GP, who will ask about symptoms. A GP can refer to a local talking therapies service, or to a specialist mental health team if needed. A person can also refer themselves directly to an NHS Talking Therapies service.
ocd.treatment: The NHS describes two main treatments: talking therapy, usually CBT, and medicine, usually an SSRI. CBT for OCD usually includes exposure and response prevention (ERP), in which a person faces an obsessive thought while holding back from the usual compulsion. Medicine may be needed if talking therapy does not help or if OCD is fairly severe. NICE public information says combined treatment of CBT with an SSRI should be offered in some cases.
ocd.prevention: The NHS says that if obsessive thoughts and compulsions affect daily life, it is worth speaking to a GP, and that a person can also refer themselves to an NHS Talking Therapies service.
ocd.seekCare: If someone is in immediate danger, or cannot keep themselves or someone else safe, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, the NHS lists NHS 111 (mental health option). Samaritans are free to call on 116 123, 24 hours a day. For OCD that keeps coming back and affects daily life, the usual route is a routine GP appointment or a self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies.

sections.heading: What is OCD and how does it feel?
sections.body:
Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental health condition in which a person has obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours. The NHS describes an obsession as an unwanted and unpleasant thought, image or urge that keeps coming into the mind and can cause feelings of anxiety, disgust or unease. A compulsion is a repetitive behaviour or mental act that a person feels they need to do to ease the distress an obsession brings.

Mind describes obsessions as starting with an unwelcome thought or feeling, often called an intrusive thought. It says the relief from a compulsion does not last: the thought pops back into the mind and the person repeats the compulsion, so the cycle repeats. OCD-UK says that symptoms can wax and wane over time. The NHS says OCD can affect men, women and children, and that women can sometimes have OCD during pregnancy or after a baby is born.

sections.heading: What do obsessions and compulsions look like?
sections.body:
Compulsions differ from person to person. The Royal College of Psychiatrists gives examples including washing, checking, touching, ordering or lining things up, counting, and thinking certain thoughts. Pages from NHS trusts also list excessive handwashing, repeated checking, excessive cleaning, counting or repeating words, and excessive praying. One NHS trust gives fears of contamination by germs or dirt as a typical theme.

Mind says compulsions can be things a person does physically, such as repeatedly checking that a door is locked, things done in the head, such as repeating a specific word, or things that involve other people, such as asking for reassurance. Mind describes asking for reassurance as a very common compulsion. NHS inform notes that not all compulsive behaviours are obvious to other people. Mind adds that people whose compulsions are mostly internal, sometimes described as having Pure O, still carry out compulsions even though they cannot be seen.

sections.heading: What causes OCD and who is affected?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says the cause of OCD is unknown, although genetics, brain biology and chemistry, and the environment may all play a role. Mind says there are different theories about why someone develops OCD, and that no theory can fully explain every person's experience. It points to personal experiences and biological factors.

The NHS says a person is more likely to develop OCD if a family member has it. It also says OCD may be more common in people who have been bullied, abused or neglected, and that it sometimes starts after an important life event, such as childbirth or a bereavement. The NHS adds that people who are neat, meticulous and methodical, with high personal standards, or who have a very strong sense of responsibility for themselves and others, may be more likely to develop OCD.

The NHS says OCD can affect men, women and children. People can have symptoms from as early as age 6, but it often begins around puberty and early adulthood.

sections.heading: How is OCD diagnosed and where can you get help?
sections.body:
The NHS says that if obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours affect daily life, it is worth speaking to a GP. The NHS describes two routes to help. One is to refer yourself directly to an NHS Talking Therapies service in England. The other is to see a GP, who will ask about symptoms and can refer to a local talking therapies service if necessary. A GP may also refer to a specialist mental health team if needed.

The NHS also says that some people with severe, long-term OCD that has been difficult to treat may be referred to a national specialist OCD service.

For children and young people, NHS child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) are another route, and a GP can explain how to reach them. Scotland and Wales use different services from England, so a person living there can ask a GP or local NHS service about the local route.

sections.heading: How is OCD treated?
sections.body:
The NHS describes talking therapy, usually cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and medicine, usually a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), a type of antidepressant, as the main treatments. Therapy for OCD is usually CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP). In ERP a person faces an obsessive thought or feared situation while holding back from the usual compulsion. The Royal College of Psychiatrists gives the example of a therapist challenging someone not to wash their hands as much.

The NHS says medicine may be needed if talking therapy does not help or if OCD is fairly severe. It also says an SSRI can take up to 12 weeks before any benefit is noticed. NHS guidance says stopping an SSRI suddenly can cause side effects, so treatment is stopped gradually with a doctor's advice.

NICE public information says combined treatment of CBT with an SSRI should be offered in some cases. A GP or specialist team can explain which options suit a particular person.

sections.heading: OCD in children and young people
sections.body:
NICE guideline CG31 covers OCD in adults, young people and children aged 8 years and older. For children and young people it says psychological treatments should be collaborative and should engage the family or carers. It also says an SSRI should be combined with concurrent CBT including ERP, and should be prescribed only after assessment and diagnosis by a child and adolescent psychiatrist.

NICE is developing an update to this guideline. Its project page lists an expected publication date of 16 February 2027, and the update is planned to remove the current lower age limit of 8 years. Until then CG31 remains the published guideline.

Healthier Together, an NHS site for families, says that if rituals take up a lot of time, cause distress, or make it hard to do things like sleeping, studying and being with friends, the first step is an appointment with a GP. OCD-UK says that giving reassurance, although well meant, can make OCD escalate over time, and that it is still important to seek help if symptoms wax and wane.

sections.heading: When should you get help, and where can you find support?
sections.body:
For OCD that keeps coming back and affects daily life, the NHS suggests speaking to a GP or referring yourself to an NHS Talking Therapies service. This is a routine appointment rather than an emergency.

If someone is in immediate danger, or cannot keep themselves or someone else safe, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, the NHS lists NHS 111 (mental health option), where a person may be able to speak to a trained professional. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123, 24 hours a day.

The NHS says the charities OCD Action, OCD-UK and TOP UK may be useful sources of support and can tell people about local groups. OCD Action and OCD-UK both run online support groups, and Mind lists TOP UK as offering self-help therapy groups for OCD, phobias and related anxiety disorders.

faqs.q: Is OCD just a need to be tidy or clean?
faqs.a: The NHS describes OCD as a mental health condition involving obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours. The thoughts are unwanted and unpleasant, and can cause anxiety, disgust or unease. Mind says compulsions can be physical, mental, or involve other people. People whose compulsions are mostly internal still carry out compulsions, even though they cannot be seen by others.

faqs.q: Can OCD be cured?
faqs.a: The US National Institute of Mental Health says there is no cure for OCD, but available treatments can help people manage their symptoms. In the UK, the NHS describes talking therapy, usually CBT, and medicine, usually an SSRI, as the main treatments. OCD-UK notes that symptoms can wax and wane over time. The NHS suggests speaking to a GP if the thoughts affect daily life.

faqs.q: Can someone get help for OCD without seeing a GP?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says a person can refer themselves directly to an NHS Talking Therapies service in England. Seeing a GP is the other route. A GP will ask about symptoms and can refer to a local talking therapies service if necessary. A GP may also refer to a specialist mental health team if needed.

faqs.q: What is exposure and response prevention?
faqs.a: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is a type of CBT that the NHS says is usually used for OCD. In ERP a person faces an obsessive thought or feared situation while holding back from the usual compulsion. The Royal College of Psychiatrists gives the example of a therapist challenging someone not to wash their hands as much.

faqs.q: Can children and young people have OCD?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says OCD can affect men, women and children. Symptoms can start from as early as age 6, but often begin around puberty and early adulthood. NICE guideline CG31 covers children aged 8 and older and says psychological treatments should engage the family or carers. Healthier Together advises a GP appointment as the first step if rituals cause distress or get in the way of daily life.

ptsd.name: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
ptsd.definition: A mental health condition that can develop after very stressful, frightening or distressing events.
ptsd.overview: PTSD is a mental health condition that can follow a very stressful, frightening or distressing event, such as a serious accident, an assault or childbirth. Re-experiencing the event through flashbacks, nightmares and distressing images is the most typical symptom. People may also avoid reminders, feel low or feel constantly on edge. Treatment is available, and talking therapies come first.
causes: Experiencing a very stressful, frightening or distressing event, or a prolonged traumatic experience.
Events linked to PTSD include serious accidents, physical or sexual assault, abuse, childbirth experiences and the death of someone close.
Seeing other people hurt or in distress during a person's job is sometimes called secondary trauma.
Complex PTSD is linked to repeated or long-term trauma.
People with PTSD have abnormal levels of stress hormones.
riskFactors: A history of depression or anxiety
Limited support from family or friends
A genetic factor may be involved
Trauma over a long period of time
signs: Hypervigilance, with constant awareness of possible threats
Jumpiness and irritability
Sleep problems
Avoiding reminders of the traumatic event
complications: Depression, emotional numbing and drug or alcohol misuse can occur alongside PTSD
Difficulties in relationships can feature in complex PTSD
ptsd.diagnosis: The NHS says a GP will ask about a person's symptoms and can refer them to a mental health specialist. NICE-based material notes that symptoms must persist beyond a month before PTSD can be diagnosed.
ptsd.treatment: The NHS lists talking therapies and medicine as the main treatments. Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are the main talking therapies. NICE says venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline should be considered for adults who prefer drug treatment. NHS 111 Wales says treatment is likely to be offered if symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks or are severe.
ptsd.prevention: NICE advises against offering drug treatments, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD in adults.
ptsd.seekCare: If a person is in immediate danger or may be about to harm themselves, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans are free to call on 116 123, 24 hours a day. NHS Inform advises contacting a GP if problems continue about 4 weeks after a traumatic experience. The NHS says people can refer themselves directly to a talking therapies service.

sections.heading: What is PTSD?
sections.body:
PTSD stands for post-traumatic stress disorder. The NHS describes it as a mental health condition that can follow a very stressful, frightening or distressing event, or a prolonged traumatic experience. It lists serious accidents, physical or sexual assault, abuse, traumatic events at work, serious health problems, childbirth experiences, the death of someone close, war and torture among the events that can lead to it. Mind adds that seeing other people hurt or in distress during a person's job is sometimes called secondary trauma.

Symptoms can begin straight after an event, or weeks, months or even years later. The NHS estimates that PTSD affects about 1 in every 3 people who have a traumatic experience, and it says it is not clear exactly why some people develop it and others do not. NHS 111 Wales says about 2 in every 3 people who have problems after a traumatic experience get better within a few weeks without treatment. Treatment is available, and talking therapies come first.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of PTSD?
sections.body:
The NHS says the most typical symptom is re-experiencing the event, which means involuntarily and vividly reliving it. This can involve flashbacks, nightmares, and repetitive, distressing images or sensations. Avoidance is also common, such as steering clear of places or conversations that remind a person of the event, and feeling numb or cut off.

NHS Scotland describes a state of being alert or on edge that includes panic when reminded of the trauma, jumpiness, irritability and sleep problems. Hypervigilance, which means constant awareness of possible threats, is part of this on-edge state. For adults, the NHS also lists finding it difficult to control feelings and emotions, low mood, and being more irritable or angry than usual. In children, the NHS describes signs that include re-enacting the trauma through play and wetting the bed, even if the child did not before the traumatic event.

sections.heading: What is complex PTSD?
sections.body:
The NHS says complex PTSD shares its core symptoms with PTSD but adds feelings of worthlessness, shame and guilt, problems controlling emotions, finding it hard to feel connected with other people, and difficulties in relationships. NHS Inform adds dissociation and risky behaviour. The NHS links complex PTSD to repeated or long-term trauma, and lists childhood abuse or neglect, domestic violence, sexual abuse, torture, sex trafficking, slavery and war as examples. Mind says people with complex PTSD may be especially prone to emotional flashbacks, in which they feel intense emotions from the original trauma, such as fear, shame, sadness or despair.

The NHS says psychological therapies used for PTSD, such as trauma-focused CBT, may be offered, and EMDR is also named. NHS Inform notes that many people need longer-term, intensive support. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says work with a therapist often happens in three stages, although a person may not need all of them or may repeat some. The first stage, stabilisation, is designed to help a person regain control over anxiety and re-experiencing symptoms, and sometimes it is the only help needed.

sections.heading: What causes PTSD and who is more likely to develop it?
sections.body:
The NHS says a history of depression or anxiety, or limited support from family or friends, can raise the chance of developing PTSD after a traumatic event. It says a genetic factor may also be involved. Mind lists trauma over a long period of time, and having little or no support from friends, family or professionals, as factors that raise the risk. For complex PTSD, the NHS notes a higher risk when the trauma happens at a young age or when the harm comes from someone close.

On the biology, the NHS says studies have shown that people with PTSD have abnormal levels of stress hormones. It also reports that parts of the brain involved in emotional processing appear different on brain scans, and that the hippocampus appears smaller in size. The NHS describes these as findings in people with PTSD, and it says it is not yet clear exactly why some people who go through a traumatic experience develop the condition while others do not.

sections.heading: How is PTSD diagnosed and treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP will ask about a person's symptoms and can refer them to a mental health specialist, such as a talking therapies service or a psychiatrist. NICE-based material notes that symptoms must persist beyond a month before PTSD can be diagnosed. NHS 111 Wales says treatment is likely to be offered if symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks or are severe, and it describes watchful waiting as monitoring symptoms to see whether they improve or get worse without treatment.

The NHS lists talking therapies and medicine as the main treatments, and trauma-focused CBT and EMDR as the main talking therapies. NICE advises offering individual trauma-focused CBT to adults who first seek help more than a month after a traumatic event, and EMDR to adults whose symptoms appear more than 3 months after a non-combat-related trauma. NICE says venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline should be considered for adults who prefer drug treatment. For children and young people, the NHS says trauma-focused CBT is usually recommended, with EMDR for those who do not respond to it. NICE advises that drug treatments should not be offered to under-18s for PTSD.

sections.heading: Living with PTSD and when to get help
sections.body:
The NHS suggests talking to a friend, family member or online support group, keeping a diary to spot triggers such as particular smells or sounds, trying breathing exercises, staying active, eating well and getting enough sleep. It advises against recreational drugs, smoking and heavy drinking. Mind's self-care page describes slow breathing, grounding techniques that keep a person connected to the present during flashbacks, and a sensory box of items that help with grounding.

NHS Inform advises contacting a GP if problems continue about 4 weeks after a traumatic experience. The NHS says people can refer themselves directly to a talking therapies service. If a person is in immediate danger or may be about to harm themselves, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans are free to call on 116 123, 24 hours a day.

faqs.q: Can PTSD get better?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says about 2 in every 3 people who develop problems after a traumatic experience get better within a few weeks without treatment. Where symptoms last longer, the NHS lists talking therapies and medicine as the main treatments, with trauma-focused CBT and EMDR the main talking therapies. A GP can ask about symptoms and refer a person to a specialist.

faqs.q: How long after a trauma can PTSD start?
faqs.a: The NHS says PTSD can develop immediately after a disturbing event, or weeks, months or even years later. NHS Inform advises contacting a GP if problems continue about 4 weeks after a traumatic experience. For a diagnosis, symptoms must persist beyond a month. NHS 111 Wales says treatment is likely to be offered if symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks or are severe.

faqs.q: What is the difference between PTSD and complex PTSD?
faqs.a: The NHS says complex PTSD shares its core symptoms with PTSD but adds feelings of worthlessness, shame and guilt, problems controlling emotions and difficulties in relationships. It is linked to repeated or long-term trauma. Psychological therapies used for PTSD, such as trauma-focused CBT, may be offered, and the Royal College of Psychiatrists says treatment often happens in stages.

faqs.q: Can children have PTSD?
faqs.a: The NHS describes signs in children that include re-enacting the trauma through play and wetting the bed, even if the child did not before the traumatic event. Trauma-focused CBT is usually recommended for children and young people, with EMDR offered to those who do not respond to it. NICE advises that drug treatments should not be offered to under-18s for the prevention or treatment of PTSD.

faqs.q: Can people get talking therapy without seeing a GP?
faqs.a: The NHS says people can refer themselves directly to a talking therapies service, so a GP referral is not always needed. If a GP thinks a person has PTSD, the GP will ask about symptoms and can refer them to a mental health specialist, such as a talking therapies service or a psychiatrist.

faqs.q: Who can someone contact in a mental health crisis?
faqs.a: In a mental health crisis, call 999 or go to A&E if there is immediate danger or someone may be about to harm themselves. NHS 111 has a mental health option for urgent help that is not an emergency. Samaritans are free to call on 116 123, 24 hours a day.

sections.heading: What is bipolar disorder and what are the episodes?
sections.body:
Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition that mainly affects mood. People with it have extreme mood changes, with high moods called mania or hypomania and low moods called depression. Hypomania is a milder form of mania. The NHS says these moods usually last a few days or weeks at a time. NHS 111 Wales says people often have stable periods with no symptoms, which can last for weeks, months or years.
During mania a person may be more irritable than usual and sleep much less than normal, according to Rethink Mental Illness. Depression can bring low energy, changes in sleep and appetite, feelings of worthlessness, poor concentration and withdrawal from other people. NHS 111 Wales also lists suicidal thoughts and thoughts of self-harm among the features of depression. Severe manic or depressive episodes can include hallucinations or delusions, which are symptoms of psychosis.

sections.heading: What types of bipolar disorder are there?
sections.body:
In bipolar I disorder, a person has at least one manic episode, and this is often accompanied by periods of deep depression. In bipolar II disorder, a person has hypomanic and major depressive episodes rather than full mania. The US National Institute of Mental Health says people with bipolar II often seek help only for depression, and their hypomania can go unnoticed.

The NHS describes cyclothymia as a mild form of bipolar disorder. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says its mood swings are less severe than those in full bipolar disorder but can last longer. The NHS says people with cyclothymia are at risk of developing full bipolar disorder, so it is important to get help before reaching this stage, and it is not known how many will go on to develop it.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists also describes mixed states, a blend of mania and depression, such as feeling very low while also restless and overactive.

sections.heading: What causes bipolar disorder, and what can trigger episodes?
sections.body:
The exact cause of bipolar disorder is not known. A review of the research describes it as highly heritable, and having a parent with the condition is considered the most important risk factor. MedlinePlus says environmental conditions likely interact with genetic factors to determine overall risk.

Childhood trauma is a recurring theme in the research. One review links childhood maltreatment to more severe and frequent mood episodes and an earlier start. Stressful life events and substance use are also associated with the condition, although it is hard to tell whether substance use leads to an episode or happens during one.

Mind lists examples of things that can trigger an episode, including stressful periods, lack of sleep, significant life events such as weddings, having a child or losing a loved one, periods of change or uncertainty, and feeling overwhelmed or busy. In a Bipolar UK survey, poor sleep was named as the biggest trigger for a first episode or a relapse.

sections.heading: How is bipolar disorder diagnosed and treated?
sections.body:
Diagnosis can take a long time. Bipolar UK's Bipolar Commission reported an average delay of about nine and a half years before people receive a diagnosis, and notes there are no physical tests for it. Mood symptoms caused by a medical condition, such as an overactive thyroid, are classed separately from bipolar disorder, and clinicians may check thyroid function to rule out a physical cause.

The NHS says bipolar disorder cannot be cured, but treatments can help manage it. The main treatments are medicines to stabilise mood and talking therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). NICE names lithium as the preferred long-term treatment. A mental health specialist works with the person to create a treatment plan, and most people have a combination of treatments that includes medication, talking therapy and lifestyle changes. The NHS says an antidepressant is not usually prescribed unless a bipolar specialist has recommended it, because antidepressants alone can lead to relapse.

sections.heading: Living with bipolar disorder
sections.body:
Mind says a regular routine can help mood feel calmer when it is high and more motivated when it is low. Getting enough sleep can help keep mood stable or shorten an episode. Gentle exercise such as yoga or swimming can help with relaxation and managing stress, and a balanced, nutritious diet can help a person feel well and think clearly.

Mind suggests noting down mood patterns in a diary or on a phone. Bipolar UK offers a free mood scale, mood diary and mood tracker app, which can help people spot their patterns, triggers and any early warning signs of a relapse. Bipolar UK also runs courses that cover mood monitoring and early warning signs plans.

Mind describes a crisis plan, best made while a person is well, that sets out what to do if early warning signs or triggers appear or the person feels very distressed.

sections.heading: When should someone get help?
sections.body:
If someone is in immediate danger or has seriously harmed themselves, for example with an overdose, or may be about to, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E. For feelings that make a person feel unsafe, distressed or worried about their mental health, the NHS lists NHS 111, which has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time of day.

NHS 111 Wales gives two situations in which to seek help: extreme mood changes that last a long time or affect everyday life, and a diagnosis where treatments are not working. It advises speaking to a mental health specialist if the person has one, and otherwise a GP. NHS Inform in Scotland says people can also phone 111 for advice if they are worried about someone else.

faqs.q: Can bipolar disorder be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says bipolar disorder cannot be cured, but there are treatments that can help manage it. The main treatments are medicines to stabilise mood and talking therapy such as CBT. A mental health specialist works with the person to create a treatment plan.

faqs.q: What is the difference between mania and hypomania?
faqs.a: Hypomania is a milder form of mania. In bipolar I disorder a person has at least one manic episode, while bipolar II involves hypomanic and major depressive episodes rather than full mania. The US National Institute of Mental Health says the hypomanic episodes in bipolar II are less severe than the manic episodes in bipolar I.

faqs.q: Does bipolar disorder run in families?
faqs.a: A research review describes bipolar disorder as highly heritable, and having a parent with the condition is considered the most important risk factor. The same review says most people with a close relative who has bipolar disorder will not develop it themselves. The exact cause is not known.

faqs.q: How long does a diagnosis take?
faqs.a: It can take a long time. Bipolar UK's Bipolar Commission reported an average delay of about nine and a half years before people receive a bipolar diagnosis, and notes there are no physical tests for it. Clinicians may check thyroid function to rule out a physical cause of mood symptoms.

faqs.q: What helps in a crisis?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if someone has seriously harmed themselves or may be about to. For feeling unsafe or distressed, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time. Mind describes a crisis plan, made in advance, that sets out what to do if early warning signs or triggers appear.

insomnia.name: Insomnia
insomnia.definition: A sleep problem in which a person regularly has trouble sleeping, including finding it hard to get to sleep or waking often in the night.
insomnia.overview: Insomnia means regularly having trouble sleeping. The NHS says people with insomnia may find it hard to go to sleep, wake several times in the night, lie awake, or wake early and be unable to get back to sleep. It can last for a short time or continue for months or years. Daytime sleepiness, tiredness and difficulty concentrating are among its effects. Stress, anxiety and depression are the most common causes, according to the NHS. Changing sleep habits often helps, and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first treatment.

If sleep problems come with thoughts of harming oneself, call 999 or go to A&E if in immediate danger. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, use NHS 111 online or call 111 and choose the mental health option. Samaritans are free to call on 116 123 at any time of day or night.
